snippets.text: On the ISS, 3-minute PVT-B reaction speed was significantly slower after 6 hours of sleep or less (Jones et al., 2022).
In NASA's ISS Cognition study, a reaction-speed score at or below 1.5 SD under a crewmember's own baseline was counted as a low score.
On the 3-minute PVT-B (1 to 4 second target gap), a reaction time of 355 ms or slower is a lapse, under 100 ms is a false start, and mean 1/RT speed is most sensitive to sleep loss.
NASA-STD-3001 provides an 8.5-hour sleep opportunity per 24 hours. On Mars transit, messages to Earth take 3 to 22 minutes each way, so urgent signs never wait for Earth.
2025 AHA/ACC categories classify blood pressure as normal (<120/<80), elevated (120-129/<80), stage 1 (130-139 or 80-89), stage 2 (>=140 or >=90), and severe hypertension (>180/120 mmHg).
For a blood pressure reading above 180/120 mmHg without warning symptoms, AHA guidance is to wait about 5 minutes and retest. If warning symptoms appear, act immediately without waiting.
NASA spaceflight standard OCHMO-STD-100.1A defines hypertension as sustained blood pressure at or above 140/90 mmHg across separate days.
In flight on the ISS (Norsk et al., 2015), 24-hour blood pressure averaged about 8/9 mmHg lower than before flight, so shifts from your own in-flight baseline stand out earlier.

NHLBI defines low blood pressure as lower than 90/60 mmHg. Dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting and confusion are warning symptoms; cold sweaty skin, rapid breathing and a weak rapid pulse are signs of shock.
CDC steps require 30 minutes without food, caffeine or exercise, an empty bladder, at least 5 minutes quiet supported rest with legs uncrossed, bare upper arm at heart level, and staying silent.
Warning symptoms such as chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, severe bleeding or collapse require alerting a crewmate immediately and opening the offline Emergency guide — never wait for Earth.
